clue.text: Drinks hard to get from vessels

indicators.note: the hard letter is taken away from the word for vessels, so this asks for a removal

parts.note: ships are seagoing vessels
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to pour drinks out of awkward containers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get from' takes H out of SHIPS.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to sip is to drink in small mouthfuls, so both words mean taking liquid.

clue.text: Phone number in broadcast at first identifying sleigh

indicators.note: the sowing piece comes first, before the phone, in the finished word
the number letter goes inside the word for broadcast

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to sow it, scattering it widely
a mobile is a mobile phone, the British name for a cellphone

explanation.surface: A radio report opens by identifying a sleigh's phone number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' means scatter seed, not transmit; 'identifying' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorised vehicle on skis or tracks for snow travel is a modern kind of sleigh.

clue.text: College poseur collapsed with the end of course

indicators.note: something collapsed has fallen into a heap, so these letters are rearranged
the final letter of the word course is taken

explanation.surface: A pretentious student at a college falls over at the end of a degree course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapsed' rearranges POSEUR and THE; 'end of' picks the E of course.
explanation.definitionFit: Peterhouse is the oldest college of Cambridge University, founded in 1284.

clue.text: Purloined six?

definitions.meaning: a cross-reference to the entry at 6-down, forgetful or absent-minded, whose sense this word shares

explanation.surface: Someone has stolen a six, perhaps from a scoreboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'six?' is not a number but the entry at 6 Down, ABSENT-MINDED; the question mark flags the cross-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstracted means both removed (stolen) and lost in thought, preoccupied like an absent-minded person.

clue.text: Urge to tuck into some meat arising on a larger scale

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters are read upwards, so reversed
the urging word is put inside the meat word, as if tucked in

parts.note: a rib is a cut of meat
to egg on is to urge

explanation.surface: An urge to eat some meat grows on a larger scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urge' is a verb here (to egg on); 'arising' reverses the whole assembly, which reads upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigger is the comparative of big, meaning greater in size or scale.

clue.text: Rugby players, perhaps forwards, missing first two when crossing line

indicators.note: the shortened word straddles the line letter, holding it within
the opening pair of letters is dropped from the attackers word

parts.note: forwards, players who go on the attack, are an example of attackers

explanation.surface: Rugby forwards fail to stop the first two runners crossing the try line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing first two' turns ATTACKERS into TACKERS; 'crossing' wraps that round L.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby, tacklers are the players who bring down an opponent carrying the ball.

clue.text: Forgetful man's indebted for correction

indicators.note: letters that need correcting are wrongly placed, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A forgetful man owes money and must put his accounts right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for correction' rearranges the letters of MAN'S INDEBTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone absent-minded is preoccupied and so tends to forget things, the plain synonym.

clue.text: Start to trim headgear, the one over there

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, taken from trim

parts.note: a hat is headgear

explanation.surface: Someone sets about trimming a hat, pointing to the one over there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start to' takes T from trim.
explanation.definitionFit: That is the demonstrative pronoun for a thing at a distance, the one not here.

clue.text: Classic lover cheated on love

parts.note: to do someone is to cheat or swindle them, so did means cheated
love is zero in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A lover from the classics was unfaithful to her love.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places DID above O.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido, Queen of Carthage, loved Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid and killed herself when he left her.

clue.text: Covers losing first crop

indicators.note: the opening letter of the covers word is dropped

parts.note: coats are covering layers, as of paint

explanation.surface: Covers are blown off a crop in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing first' drops the C of COATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oats are a cereal grain grown as a farm crop.

clue.text: Sweet treat, say, good thing to chew — excellent when swallowed

parts.note: e.g., for example, is signalled by say

indicators.note: the excellent word is swallowed by the chewing word, ending up inside it

parts.note: cud is what a cow chews
star used as an adjective means excellent

explanation.surface: A sweet, good, chewy treat, excellent once swallowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thing to chew' is the cud a cow chews; 'when swallowed' signals that the excellent word goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg custard is a baked dessert of eggs, milk and sugar, a sweet pudding.

clue.text: Bullfighting's foremost idol working with learner bullfighter

indicators.note: the foremost letter of the bullfighting word is taken
working here means being worked into a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A famous matador teams up with a novice in the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foremost' picks B; 'working' rearranges IDOL and LEARNER.
explanation.definitionFit: A banderillero is the bullfighter who plants banderillas, barbed darts, in the bull's neck.

clue.text: Could primarily be a man and a girl not getting it together properly?

definitions.text: Could primarily be a man and a girl not getting it together properly?

indicators.note: letters that do not come together properly are disordered, so they are rearranged
primarily means first, so the opening letter of could is taken

explanation.surface: A man and a woman fail to make their relationship work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not getting it together properly' rearranges BE A MAN A GIRL; 'primarily' adds C. Read whole, the clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mariage blanc, French for white marriage, is one never consummated, with the couple never physically together.

clue.text: Sadly, much as I do to secure profit, ultimately … I haven't got this

indicators.note: the jumbled letters close around and hold the final letter of profit
sadly here means badly or poorly, so these letters are jumbled
ultimately means at the last, so the final letter of profit is taken

explanation.surface: A frustrated speaker complains that, for all their effort, profit never comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' rearranges MUCH AS I DO; 'to secure' wraps the jumble round T, from 'ultimately' on profit.
explanation.definitionFit: King Midas turned all he touched to gold, so someone who fails to make money lacks that gift.

clue.text: Set aside for use in speculation when prices fall

indicators.note: the setting-aside word is put to use inside the gamble word

parts.note: a bet is a speculation, a gamble
to earmark is to set aside for a purpose

explanation.surface: Money is set aside for speculating during a falling stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a clause, not a noun: a bear market is defined by the time when prices fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear market is a period of falling share prices, named for the bear swiping downwards.

clue.text: Expressing moods by embracing cross

indicators.note: the two letters of by hold the cross word between them

parts.note: a rood is a crucifix, a cross in a church

explanation.surface: Someone shows their moods by hugging a cross person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' is not angry but the rood, a church crucifix.
explanation.definitionFit: Broody means sullen and moody, given to sulking and brooding.

clue.text: Prescribed way shows bouncer throwing out naval man

indicators.note: the naval officer's letters are thrown out of the bouncing word

parts.note: a trampoline is something one bounces on
PO is the abbreviation for petty officer, a naval rank

explanation.surface: A nightclub doorman shows the set route by ejecting a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bouncer' looks like a doorman but is a trampoline.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively tramlines are a fixed course that must be followed, like a tram on its rails.

clue.text: High point is capturing ash, say, in smokiness of whisky

indicators.note: the high point word holds the tree word inside it, as a captive

parts.note: a peak is a high point
an ash is an example of a tree

explanation.surface: A highland summit captures ash from the smoke of a whisky still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ash' is not cinders but the tree, flagged by 'say'.
explanation.definitionFit: Peat reek is the smoke of burning peat, and the smoky flavour it gives Scotch whisky.

clue.text: "Look! Snake without tail" (one points)

parts.note: la is an old exclamation meaning look or see

indicators.note: the last letter, the tail, of the snake word is cut off

parts.note: a serpent is a snake

explanation.surface: Someone cries out at a tailless snake while another points at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without tail' drops the T of SERPENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser pen is a pointer used by lecturers to highlight things on a screen.

clue.text: Good weather not initially without rain? That's not right

indicators.note: the opening letter of the sunshine word is not used

parts.note: sun, sunshine, counts as good weather
fair weather is dry, without rain; the question mark admits the loose fit

explanation.surface: A grumble that good weather came, but rain did not, which is unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not initially' drops the S of SUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfair means unjust, and an exclamation of not right is a protest at injustice.

clue.text: Poor actor, out of touch, right at bottom of heap?

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom is the end, so the right letter is shifted there

parts.note: remote means distant, out of touch

explanation.surface: A bad, out-of-touch actor finds himself at the bottom of the pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at bottom of heap' moves the R of REMOTE to the foot of the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An emoter overdoes emotion on stage, a ham, which makes an unflattering name for a poor actor.

clue.text: Character in Greek play mucked up calmest entry

indicators.note: something mucked up has been messed up, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: An actor in a Greek tragedy botches the quietest entrance onstage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mucked up' rearranges CALMEST ENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon, murders him in Aeschylus's tragedy Agamemnon.

clue.text: Note and other notes picked up as an opener

indicators.note: in a down clue, picked up means lifted, so the letters read upwards in reverse

parts.note: a wad is a thick bundle of banknotes

explanation.surface: A musical note and others are taken up as an opening phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'notes' are banknotes, not music; 'picked up' reverses N and WAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Dawn is the opening of the day, and figuratively the beginning of anything.

clue.text: Inexplicably popular League in version of movie

indicators.note: the league letter goes inside the film word

parts.note: a cut, such as a director's cut, is a version of a film

explanation.surface: A movie is inexplicably popular in one version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'League' is just its abbreviation L.
explanation.definitionFit: A cult film or band has a devoted following out of proportion to its wider fame.

clue.text: Resort attractions employ blokes in small quantities?

indicators.note: the employ and blokes words go inside the quantities word

parts.note: amts is a shortened, small form of amounts; the question mark flags the joke
to employ is to use
blokes is British slang for men

explanation.surface: Seaside attractions hire men in small numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small quantities?' means amounts written small, AMTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusements are the arcades and rides that draw visitors to a British seaside resort.

clue.text: Avoid love

definitions.meaning: to ... something is to dodge it
a zero score in cricket, and love is zero in tennis; also a British term of endearment

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman out for no runs scores a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck is to dodge, and a duck in cricket is nothing, the same as love.

clue.text: Businessmen with contacts knew resort needs redevelopment

indicators.note: a redeveloped site is rebuilt in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Business people with connections knew the resort had to be rebuilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redevelopment' rearranges KNEW RESORT; 'needs' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Networkers build and use webs of contacts for business advantage.

clue.text: Go second in heat?

parts.note: an animal in heat is ready to mate, which slang calls hot

explanation.surface: An athlete goes second in a race heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heat' looks like a race round, but 'in heat' means hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A go, as in having a go at something, is an attempt or a shot.
